title: Hungary Beats England 6-3 at Wembley
text:
On 25 November 1953 England met Hungary at Wembley. England had never lost a home match to a team from outside the British Isles, and much of the English press expected the visitors to be taught a lesson. Hungary, the Olympic champions, had gone unbeaten for over three years under coach Gusztav Sebes.

The match was over as a contest within half an hour. Nandor Hidegkuti scored in the first minute. Wearing the number 9 shirt of a centre forward, he dropped back into midfield instead of staying up front, and England's centre half, used to marking a striker, did not know whether to follow him. Hungary's forwards and midfielders swapped positions constantly and passed the ball quickly in short combinations. Ferenc Puskas scored one goal after dragging the ball back with the sole of his boot, leaving England's captain Billy Wright sliding past him.

Hungary won 6 to 3, with Hidegkuti scoring three. The players had been drilled as a unit, many of them together at the same club, Honved, and they played a system in which every man understood the others' movements. England's players were skilled, but they played in fixed positions.

Six months later, in Budapest, Hungary beat England again, 7 to 1. The Wembley defeat forced English football to rethink its training, tactics and attitudes to the rest of the world.
lesson: A team whose members understand each other's movements can outplay individually strong opponents stuck in fixed roles. Flexible, shared systems beat rigid positions.
people: Ferenc Puskas, Nandor Hidegkuti, Gusztav Sebes, Billy Wright
source: Contemporary match reports; Jonathan Wilson, Inverting the Pyramid (2008)
